claim: The improved annotation pipeline was applied to 9599 Pseudomonas genomes, of which 94% were draft genomes.
source: We applied our improved pyoverdine biosynthesis annotation pipeline to 9599 Pseudomonas genomes (including 613 complete and 8986 draft genomes) retrieved from the Pseudomonas Genome Database (Winsor et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of genomes analyzed and their composition.

claim: The pyoverdine biosynthesis machinery was found in 97% of the analyzed Pseudomonas genomes.
source: We found the pyoverdine biosynthesis machinery in 97% of the genomes (Figure 2b), indicating that the machinery is ubiquitous in Pseudomonas.
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage of genomes containing pyoverdine biosynthesis machinery based on their analysis and references Figure 2b.

claim: The pyoverdine biosynthesis machinery was likely truncated in 63.4% (6087) of the genomes due to draft genome fragmentation.
source: However, since 94% of the analyzed genomes were in draft form, the pyoverdine biosynthesis machinery was likely truncated (i.e. on the edge of the contig) in 63.4% (6087) of the genomes.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages and numbers of truncated genomes based on their analysis.

claim: Around 3.1% of retained genomes (293) were missing pyoverdine synthetic genes and classified as 'non-producers'.
source: Around 3.1% of retained genomes (293) with high assembly completeness were missing pyoverdine synthetic genes, indicating that these Pseudomonas strains were not able to produce pyoverdine ('non-producers').
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the percentage and number of non-producer genomes.

claim: 33.5% (3219 genomes) were classified as 'producers' with complete pyoverdine NRPS assembly lines.
source: The rest of the genomes (33.5%; 3219 genomes) were classified as 'producers' with complete pyoverdine NRPS assembly lines that meet all our quality controls.
evidence: The manuscript provides the percentage and number of producer genomes.

claim: The lengths of pyoverdine synthetic clusters ranged between 7690 and 21,333 amino acids.
source: The lengths of pyoverdine synthetic clusters ranged between 7690 and 21,333 amino acids, and the number of A domains per synthetase ranged between 6 and 17, with a total of 35,281 A domains being present across all strains (Figure 2c).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific ranges for cluster lengths based on their analysis and references Figure 2c.

claim: The number of A domains per synthetase ranged between 6 and 17.
source: The lengths of pyoverdine synthetic clusters ranged between 7690 and 21,333 amino acids, and the number of A domains per synthetase ranged between 6 and 17, with a total of 35,281 A domains being present across all strains (Figure 2c).
evidence: The manuscript reports the range of A domains per synthetase based on their analysis.

claim: A total of 35,281 A domains were present across all producer strains.
source: The lengths of pyoverdine synthetic clusters ranged between 7690 and 21,333 amino acids, and the number of A domains per synthetase ranged between 6 and 17, with a total of 35,281 A domains being present across all strains (Figure 2c).
evidence: The manuscript provides the total count of A domains identified.

claim: After data cleaning, 1928 Pseudomonas strains were retained, segregating into 1664 pyoverdine producers and 264 non-producers.
source: This data cleaning yielded a total of 1928 Pseudomonas strains (403 complete and 1525 incomplete genomes), segregating into 1664 pyoverdine producers and 264 non-producers.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the final number of strains after data cleaning.

claim: The number of Pseudomonas aeruginosa A domains ranges between 7 and 14.
source: For example, the number of Pseudomonas aeruginosa A domains ranges between 7 and 14.
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific example of A domain variation within a species.

claim: 101 A domains linked to 13 experimentally confirmed amino acid substrates were identified from 13 known pyoverdines.
source: From this dataset, we could identify 101 A domains that are linked to 13 experimentally confirmed amino acid substrates (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript states the number of A domains and substrates in the reference dataset.

claim: The full A domain sequence is not informative for substrate prediction.
source: We found that the full A domain sequence is not informative for substrate prediction (Figure 3b, left panel).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references Figure 3b.

claim: Information-rich positions for substrate prediction start with motif A4 and end before motif A5.
source: Instead, our analysis indicated that information-rich positions start with motif A4 and end before motif A5, consistent with the known role of the A domain pocket in substrate selectivity (He et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript reports the specific motif regions identified as informative and cites supporting literature.

claim: The sequence region from motifs A4 to A5 (Amotif4-5), in conjunction with Jukes-Cantor distance and Ward linkage clustering, performed best in accurately distinguishing between different substrates.
source: Overall, the sequence region from motifs A4 to A5 (termed 'Amotif4-5'), in conjunction with Jukes-Cantor distance and Ward linkage clustering, performed best in accurately distinguishing between different substrates and maintaining homogeneity for identical substrates (Figure 3b).
evidence: The manuscript reports the best-performing parameter combination based on their analysis.

claim: The phylogeny-focused method can find and correct previously misclassified substrate information of A domains in the MIBiG database.
source: To our delight, our method can find and correct previously misclassified substrate information of A domains in the MIBiG database (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The manuscript states that their method identified errors in the MIBiG database and references supporting figures.

claim: 20 pyoverdine-producing Pseudomonas strains were sequenced for experimental validation.
source: To test whether our bioinformatic pipeline can reliably predict pyoverdine structures, we sequenced the genomes of 20 pyoverdine-producing Pseudomonas strains previously isolated from soil and water (Butaitė et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental validation approach with 20 strains.

claim: None of the 20 predicted pyoverdine structures matched any of the 13 reference pyoverdine structures.
source: Notably, none of the predicted structures matched any of the 13 reference pyoverdine structures, and 9 out of the 20 structures were predicted to be novel (not yet characterized) pyoverdines.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that none of the validation structures matched the reference structures.

claim: 9 out of the 20 predicted structures were novel (not yet characterized) pyoverdines.
source: Notably, none of the predicted structures matched any of the 13 reference pyoverdine structures, and 9 out of the 20 structures were predicted to be novel (not yet characterized) pyoverdines.
evidence: The manuscript states the number of novel pyoverdines predicted.

claim: A near-perfect match (94.4%) was found between the predicted and observed pyoverdine chemical structures, with 151 out of 160 amino acids accurately assigned.
source: We found a near-perfect match (94.4%) between the predicted and the observed pyoverdine chemical structures and were able to accurately assign amino acids in 151 out of 160 cases (Figure 3d).
evidence: The manuscript reports the accuracy of their predictions based on experimental validation.

claim: The phylogeny-focused method demonstrated substantial improvement compared to antiSMASH 7.0, which could only accurately assign 94 out of 160 amino acids (accuracy: 58.8%).
source: Our method demonstrated a substantial improvement compared to commonly used approaches or platforms integrating several methods (Supplementary file 6), such as antiSMASH 7.0 (Blin et al., 2023), which could only accurately assign 94 out of 160 amino acids (accuracy: 58.8%).
evidence: The manuscript compares their method's performance to antiSMASH with specific accuracy metrics.

claim: In three cases (1.9%), the algorithm could not distinguish between the substrates lysine and ornithine.
source: In three cases (1.9%), our algorithm could not distinguish between the substrates lysine and ornithine, as these two amino acids are highly similar in terms of both their chemical structures and corresponding A domain sequences.
evidence: The manuscript describes a specific limitation of their method with quantification.

claim: In four cases (2.5%), the technique assigned an 'unknown' substrate to amino acids that turned out to be valine, citrulline, and histidine.
source: In four cases (2.5%), our technique assigned an 'unknown' substrate to amino acids that turned out to be valine, citrulline, and histidine.
evidence: The manuscript reports cases where the method identified unknown substrates.

claim: Citrulline has never been reported in pyoverdines before.
source: Indeed, these three amino acids were not yet present in our reference dataset and therefore no correct prediction was possible. While citrulline has never been reported in pyoverdines before, valine has been found in a pyoverdine structure but no sequence data from the corresponding strain was available.
evidence: The manuscript states that citrulline is a novel substrate in pyoverdines.

claim: There were only two cases (0.8%) that represented true mismatches between observed and predicted amino acids.
source: Finally, there were only two cases (0.8%) that represented true mismatches between observed and predicted amino acids.
evidence: The manuscript quantifies the true error rate of their method.

claim: The pipeline achieved 83% prediction accuracy for Burkholderiales NRPS metabolites, higher than antiSMASH 7.0's 67% accuracy.
source: We observed that our pipeline consistently yields high prediction accuracy within Burkholderiales (83%), which is considerably higher than the accuracy obtained with antiSMASH 7.0 (Blin et al., 2023, 67%, Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 9).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative accuracy metrics for Burkholderiales analysis.

claim: The bioinformatic pipeline predicted the substrates of 17,880 A domains (97.75%) without ambiguity.
source: Across all assembly lines, we were able to predict the substrates of 17,880 A domains (97.75%) without ambiguity, whereas 133 A domains (0.73%) were associated with two different substrates, and 279 A domains (1.52%) predicted an unknown substrate (similar to the cases of valine and citrulline above).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number and percentage of unambiguous substrate predictions.

claim: 133 A domains (0.73%) were associated with two different substrates.
source: Across all assembly lines, we were able to predict the substrates of 17,880 A domains (97.75%) without ambiguity, whereas 133 A domains (0.73%) were associated with two different substrates, and 279 A domains (1.52%) predicted an unknown substrate (similar to the cases of valine and citrulline above).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number and percentage of ambiguous predictions.

claim: 279 A domains (1.52%) predicted an unknown substrate.
source: Across all assembly lines, we were able to predict the substrates of 17,880 A domains (97.75%) without ambiguity, whereas 133 A domains (0.73%) were associated with two different substrates, and 279 A domains (1.52%) predicted an unknown substrate (similar to the cases of valine and citrulline above).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number and percentage of unknown substrate predictions.

claim: The prediction yielded 188 different pyoverdine molecules, of which only 37 structures had been previously reported.
source: Our prediction yielded 188 different pyoverdine molecules, out of which only 37 structures had been previously reported.
evidence: The manuscript reports the total number of predicted pyoverdines and how many were previously known.

claim: The 37 previously reported pyoverdine structures were highly abundant across strains (1103 out of 1664).
source: While these 37 reported structures were highly abundant across strains (1103 out of 1664), our pipeline was powerful in identifying many of the rarer pyoverdine variants.
evidence: The manuscript reports the abundance of previously known pyoverdine structures.

claim: The fluorophore is highly conserved among the 188 predicted pyoverdine structures.
source: Agreeing with previous studies, we observed that the fluorophore is highly conserved among the 188 predicted structures.
evidence: The manuscript reports conservation of the fluorophore component.

claim: 13 amino acids form the main structural substrates of all the 188 pyoverdine structures.
source: Moreover, our analysis found that 13 amino acids form the main structural substrates of all the 188 pyoverdine structures, with most of the variation being attributable to different substrate combinations, peptide lengths, and substrate chirality (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of main amino acid substrates identified.

claim: Pyoverdine structural diversity was not strongly linked to phylogeny.
source: Notably, pyoverdine structural diversity was not strongly linked to phylogeny because the same pyoverdine structure could be found in completely unrelated species, while closely related species often had different pyoverdine structures (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the lack of correlation between pyoverdine structure and phylogeny.

claim: The same pyoverdine structure could be found in completely unrelated species.
source: Notably, pyoverdine structural diversity was not strongly linked to phylogeny because the same pyoverdine structure could be found in completely unrelated species, while closely related species often had different pyoverdine structures (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of pyoverdine distribution across phylogeny.

claim: Closely related species often had different pyoverdine structures.
source: Notably, pyoverdine structural diversity was not strongly linked to phylogeny because the same pyoverdine structure could be found in completely unrelated species, while closely related species often had different pyoverdine structures (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of pyoverdine variation within closely related species.

claim: There may be both frequent recombination and horizontal gene transfer of pyoverdine synthetase clusters between species.
source: These observations suggest that there may be both frequent recombination and horizontal gene transfer of pyoverdine synthetase clusters between species.
evidence: The manuscript infers evolutionary mechanisms from the observed distribution patterns.

claim: The bioinformatics methods developed can predict 151 novel pyoverdine candidate variants.
source: Taken together, the bioinformatics methods developed in our study can predict a suit of secondary metabolites (pyoverdines) from sequence data with high accuracy, revealing an unprecedented richness and evolutionary history of siderophores within pseudomonads and the discovery of 151 novel pyoverdine candidate variants.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of novel pyoverdine variants discovered.

claim: FpvA is a TonB-dependent receptor that transports ferri-pyoverdine into the periplasm.
source: In pseudomonads, iron-loaded pyoverdines are recognized by FpvA, a TonB-dependent receptor, that transports the ferri-pyoverdine into the periplasm (Cobessi et al., 2005; Butaitė et al., 2017; Kramer et al., 2020; Jin et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript describes the function of FpvA and cites supporting literature.

claim: The protein structure of characterized FpvA variants consists of three domains: STN, Plug, and TonB.
source: The protein structure of characterized FpvA variants consists of three domains: The Secretin and TonB N-terminus short domain (STN), the Plug domain (Plug), and the TonB-dependent receptor domain (TonB) (Cobessi et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript describes the domain structure of FpvA and cites supporting literature.

claim: All 35 reference siderophore receptor sequences share a similar length of around 800 amino acids.
source: We found that all receptor sequences share a similar length of around 800 amino acids (FpvA and FpvB sequences: 809±10 amino acids).
evidence: The manuscript reports the length characteristics of receptor sequences.

claim: FpvA and FpvB sequences have a length of 809±10 amino acids.
source: We found that all receptor sequences share a similar length of around 800 amino acids (FpvA and FpvB sequences: 809±10 amino acids).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific length measurements for FpvA and FpvB.

claim: FpvA identification based on full sequence distances is unachievable due to substantial divergence between FpvA variants.
source: We found substantial divergence between FpvA variants to an extent that was comparable to the distance between FpvA and other siderophore receptors. Moreover, FpvB variants clustered with FpvA variants, showing that FpvA identification based on full sequence distances is unachievable.
evidence: The manuscript reports the limitation of full-sequence approaches based on their analysis.

claim: The four regions with the highest FpvA identification scores all located near the Plug domain surrounding the pyoverdine transmission channel.
source: We found that the four regions with the top discrimination capacities all located near the Plug domain surrounding the pyoverdine transmission channel (Figure 6e).
evidence: The manuscript reports the location of informative sequence regions.

claim: The plug domain is known to undergo conformational changes and is involved in pyoverdine selectivity and import.
source: The plug domain is known to undergo conformational changes and is involved in pyoverdine selectivity and import (Schalk et al., 2012; Greenwald et al., 2009), suggesting that the four high-score regions are responsible for pyoverdine specificity.
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on plug domain function.

claim: The feature sequence could characterize 98% of the distance matrix compared to the whole sequence.
source: The feature sequence could characterize 98% of the distance matrix compared to the whole sequence (1534 FpvAs, r=0.98, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and substantially reduced within-group distance.
evidence: The manuscript reports the performance of the feature sequence approach.

claim: The analysis identified 4547 FpvAs, 615 FpvBs, and 9139 other TonB-dependent Fpv-like receptors across the dataset.
source: The analysis identified 4547 FpvAs, 615 FpvBs, and 9139 other TonB-dependent Fpv-like receptors across the dataset (Figure 6a).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of each receptor type identified.

claim: The 4547 FpvA sequences clustered hierarchically into 114 groups, defined by an identity threshold of 60%.
source: The 4547 FpvA sequences clustered hierarchically into 114 groups, defined by an identity threshold of 60%.
evidence: The manuscript reports the clustering results for FpvA sequences.

claim: 2293 FpvA sequences have close homologues in the reference database, while 2254 FpvA sequences lack such close homologues (sequence identity <50%).
source: When comparing to the 21 reference FpvAs (Figure 6b), we found that 2293 FpvA sequences have close homologues in the reference database, while 2254 FpvA sequences lack such close homologues (sequence identity <50%).
evidence: The manuscript reports the distribution of FpvA sequences relative to reference sequences.

claim: 2254 FpvA sequences termed as 'dissimilar to reference' may represent novel subtypes of FpvA receptors.
source: These latter sequences, termed as 'dissimilar to reference', may represent novel subtypes of FpvA receptors that could not be found by simple homology search.
evidence: The manuscript infers that dissimilar sequences represent novel receptor types.

claim: 92% of the nearest FpvA genes were located within 20 kb of their pyoverdine Pep genes.
source: In contrast, 92% of the nearest FpvA genes were indeed located within 20 kb of their pyoverdine Pep genes (Figure 6d, called proximate receptors).
evidence: The manuscript reports the genomic proximity of FpvA genes to pyoverdine synthetase genes.

claim: Single-linkage clustering with an identity threshold of 70% revealed a total of 94 FpvA groups, out of which 43 groups contained more than 10 members.
source: Single-linkage clustering with an identity threshold of 70% revealed a total of 94 groups, out of which 43 groups contained more than 10 members (Figure 6f).
evidence: The manuscript reports the clustering results for all FpvA sequences.

claim: Only three groups of FpvAs have previously been reported.
source: The diversity of receptors is hence much larger than currently anticipated as only three groups of FpvAs have previously been reported.
evidence: The manuscript compares their findings to previously known FpvA diversity.

claim: Clades with P. aeruginosa and Pseudomonas syringae species had lower FpvA diversity (1.55 and 1.60) than clades containing Pseudomonas putida and Pseudomonas fluorescens species (4.82 and 3.77).
source: We noticed large differences in FpvA diversity across the clades and species: clades with P. aeruginosa and Pseudomonas syringae species had lower FpvAs diversity (1.55 and 1.60) than clades containing Pseudomonas putida and Pseudomonas fluorescens species (4.82 and 3.77).
evidence: The manuscript reports diversity metrics for different phylogenetic clades.

claim: 31,936 receptors passed the R1 and R2 thresholds in the search across >30,000 complete bacterial genomes in NCBI.
source: We found 31,936 receptors to pass the R1 and R2 thresholds (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), and surprisingly found that FpvA receptors seem to be widely dispersed across 12,944 strains spanning 13 phyla, 22 classes, 54 orders, 139 families, 468 genera, and 2598 species (Figure 6—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 11).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of extended FpvA search across bacterial genomes.

claim: FpvA receptors seem to be widely dispersed across 12,944 strains spanning 13 phyla, 22 classes, 54 orders, 139 families, 468 genera, and 2598 species.
source: We found 31,936 receptors to pass the R1 and R2 thresholds (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), and surprisingly found that FpvA receptors seem to be widely dispersed across 12,944 strains spanning 13 phyla, 22 classes, 54 orders, 139 families, 468 genera, and 2598 species (Figure 6—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 11).
evidence: The manuscript reports the taxonomic distribution of FpvA receptors.

claim: Pseudomonas remains the genus with the highest distribution of FpvAs.
source: While Pseudomonas remains the genus with the highest distribution of FpvAs, other genera with notable distributions comprise Escherichia, Salmonella, Enterobacter, Acinetobacter, Xanthomonas, Bordetella, and Achromobacter.
evidence: The manuscript reports the relative distribution of FpvAs across genera.

claim: Other genera with notable FpvA distributions comprise Escherichia, Salmonella, Enterobacter, Acinetobacter, Xanthomonas, Bordetella, and Achromobacter.
source: While Pseudomonas remains the genus with the highest distribution of FpvAs, other genera with notable distributions comprise Escherichia, Salmonella, Enterobacter, Acinetobacter, Xanthomonas, Bordetella, and Achromobacter.
evidence: The manuscript lists genera with notable FpvA distributions.

claim: FpvA receptors for pyoverdine uptake may be widely distributed throughout the bacterial kingdom.
source: While confirmatory experimental work is still pending, these analyses suggest that FpvA receptors for pyoverdine uptake may be widely distributed throughout the bacterial kingdom.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the broad distribution of FpvA based on their analysis.

claim: Precise sequence-to-function mapping remains challenging because neither function nor substrate specificity of biosynthesis enzymes can accurately be predicted.
source: While tools exist to identify secondary metabolite clusters in genomes, precise sequence-to-function mapping remains challenging because neither function nor substrate specificity of biosynthesis enzymes can accurately be predicted.
evidence: The manuscript states a key challenge in the field.

claim: The pipeline predicted 188 chemically different pyoverdines with nearly 100% structural accuracy.
source: Our pipeline predicted 188 chemically different pyoverdines with nearly 100% structural accuracy and the presence of 94 distinct receptor groups required for the uptake of iron-loaded pyoverdines.
evidence: The abstract summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: The pipeline predicted the presence of 94 distinct receptor groups required for the uptake of iron-loaded pyoverdines.
source: Our pipeline predicted 188 chemically different pyoverdines with nearly 100% structural accuracy and the presence of 94 distinct receptor groups required for the uptake of iron-loaded pyoverdines.
evidence: The abstract summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: The pipeline unveils 151 new pyoverdine structures.
source: Our pipeline unveils an enormous yet overlooked diversity of siderophores (151 new structures) and receptors (91 new groups).
evidence: The abstract summarizes the discovery of novel structures.

claim: The pipeline unveils 91 new receptor groups.
source: Our pipeline unveils an enormous yet overlooked diversity of siderophores (151 new structures) and receptors (91 new groups).
evidence: The abstract summarizes the discovery of novel receptor groups.

claim: The approach, combining feature sequence with phylogenetic approaches, is extendable to other metabolites and microbial genera.
source: Our approach, combining feature sequence with phylogenetic approaches, is extendable to other metabolites and microbial genera, and thus emerges as powerful tool to reconstruct bacterial secondary metabolism pathways based on sequence data.
evidence: The abstract states the generalizability of the approach.

claim: Most secondary metabolites are produced by pathways comprised of modular enzymes such as non-ribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) or polyketide synthases (PKS).
source: First, most secondary metabolites are produced by pathways comprised of modular enzymes such as non-ribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) or polyketide synthases (PKS) (Andryukov et al., 2019; Kautsar et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript describes a characteristic of secondary metabolite biosynthesis and cites supporting literature.

claim: Locating complete biosynthesis clusters and identifying all enzyme-encoding genes is challenging from highly fragmented metagenomic sequences or draft genomes with a high number of contigs.
source: Locating complete biosynthesis clusters and identifying all enzyme-encoding genes is challenging from highly fragmented metagenomic sequences or draft genomes with a high number of contigs.
evidence: The manuscript describes a technical challenge in the field.

claim: A large pool of non-proteinogenic amino acids is used as substrates in NRPS biosynthesis.
source: The main challenge is that a large pool of non-proteinogenic amino acids is used as substrates and the specificity of an enzyme's A domain, connecting these unusual amino acids, is often poorly understood (He et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript describes a challenge in substrate prediction and cites supporting literature.

claim: The specificity of an enzyme's A domain, connecting unusual amino acids, is often poorly understood.
source: The main challenge is that a large pool of non-proteinogenic amino acids is used as substrates and the specificity of an enzyme's A domain, connecting these unusual amino acids, is often poorly understood (He et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript describes a knowledge gap in the field and cites supporting literature.

claim: Each Pseudomonas strain produces a single type of pyoverdine.
source: While each Pseudomonas strain produces a single type of pyoverdine, an enormous structural diversity has been described across strains and species (Cobessi et al., 2005; Diggle and Whiteley, 2020; Meyer et al., 1997; Bodilis et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript states a characteristic of pyoverdine production and cites supporting literature.

claim: An enormous structural diversity of pyoverdines has been described across strains and species.
source: While each Pseudomonas strain produces a single type of pyoverdine, an enormous structural diversity has been described across strains and species (Cobessi et al., 2005; Diggle and Whiteley, 2020; Meyer et al., 1997; Bodilis et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript describes known pyoverdine diversity and cites supporting literature.

claim: Pyoverdine types differ in their peptide backbone.
source: Pyoverdine types differ in their peptide backbone, meaning that the diversity should be mirrored in NRPS enzyme diversity and their selectivity for the different amino acid substrates (Hopkinson and Morel, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural variation in pyoverdines and cites supporting literature.

claim: Pyoverdine diversity should be mirrored in NRPS enzyme diversity and their selectivity for different amino acid substrates.
source: Pyoverdine types differ in their peptide backbone, meaning that the diversity should be mirrored in NRPS enzyme diversity and their selectivity for the different amino acid substrates (Hopkinson and Morel, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript infers a relationship between pyoverdine and enzyme diversity, citing supporting literature.

claim: Receptor diversity matches pyoverdine diversity.
source: Pyoverdine receptors are annotated as FpvA and it is known that receptor diversity matches pyoverdine diversity (Bodilis et al., 2009; Kümmerli, 2023).
evidence: The manuscript states a known relationship between receptor and pyoverdine diversity, citing supporting literature.

claim: FpvA belongs to the family of TonB-dependent receptors.
source: Moreover, FpvA belongs to the family of TonB-dependent receptors and a single Pseudomonas species often has multiple gene copies encoding different receptors.
evidence: The manuscript describes the classification of FpvA.

claim: A single Pseudomonas species often has multiple gene copies encoding different receptors.
source: Moreover, FpvA belongs to the family of TonB-dependent receptors and a single Pseudomonas species often has multiple gene copies encoding different receptors.
evidence: The manuscript describes a characteristic of receptor gene distribution.

claim: Certain receptor groups are widely distributed among Pseudomonas strains, opening the possibility of pyoverdine sharing and exploitation across strain and species boundaries.
source: Not only did our method unveil a substantial number of previously unrecognized pyoverdine receptors, but it also revealed that certain receptor groups are widely distributed among Pseudomonas strains, opening the possibility of pyoverdine sharing and exploitation across the strain and species boundaries.
evidence: The manuscript infers ecological implications from the observed receptor distribution.

claim: The pyoverdine molecule is composed of a conserved fluorescent chromophore (Flu) and a peptide chain (Pep), which are both synthesized by NRPS enzymes.
source: The pyoverdine molecules is composed of a conserved fluorescent chromophore (Flu) and a peptide chain (Pep), which are both synthesized by NRPS enzymes (Meyer, 2000).
evidence: The manuscript describes the structure of pyoverdine and cites supporting literature.

claim: AntiSMASH can recognize and annotate certain genes of an NRPS cluster, but the precise reconstruction of a complete NRPS assembly line often fails.
source: However, antiSMASH (and other popular annotation platforms; Xu et al., 2023; Keller, 2019) rely on accurate gene predictions, which are typically problematic for fragmented genomes. Consequently, while antiSMASH can recognize and annotate certain genes of an NRPS cluster, the precise reconstruction of a complete NRPS assembly line often fails.
evidence: The manuscript describes limitations of existing tools.

claim: Most available genomes are drafts and any analysis suffers from the unavoidable issue of incomplete or misannotation of gene fragments.
source: This is particularly problematic because most available genomes are drafts and any analysis suffers from the unavoidable issue of incomplete or misannotation of gene fragments.
evidence: The manuscript describes a general challenge in genomic analysis.

claim: In most cases (~90%), there are two separate biosynthetic gene clusters for Flu and Pep.
source: In most cases (~90%), there are two separate biosynthetic gene clusters for Flu and Pep. Their ordering is easy as Flu always precedes Pep.
evidence: The manuscript describes the typical organization of pyoverdine biosynthetic gene clusters.

claim: Flu always precedes Pep in the gene cluster ordering.
source: In most cases (~90%), there are two separate biosynthetic gene clusters for Flu and Pep. Their ordering is easy as Flu always precedes Pep.
evidence: The manuscript describes the ordering rule for biosynthetic gene clusters.

claim: In the remaining cases (~10%), there is either one or three biosynthetic gene clusters.
source: In the remaining cases (~10%), there is either one or three biosynthetic gene clusters. No ordering is required for the former. For the latter, we put Flu first and the cluster with TE domain at the end.
evidence: The manuscript describes alternative gene cluster organizations.

claim: At least 73 pyoverdine structures have been reported to date.
source: To date, at least 73 pyoverdine structures have been reported (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript states the number of previously known pyoverdine structures.

claim: 13 cases were identified for which both structures (obtained from structural analysis experiments) and completely sequenced synthetase genes were available.
source: Among those, we could identify 13 cases for which both structures (obtained from structural analysis experiments, we wanted to avoid any form of biases that bioinformatic pre-predictions could introduce to downstream analyses) and completely sequenced synthetase genes were available (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes the reference dataset used for method development.

claim: The A domain of each module selects for a single substrate among 22 proteinogenic and hundreds of non-proteinogenic amino acids.
source: The A domain of each module selects for a single substrate among 22 proteinogenic and hundreds of non-proteinogenic amino acids (Felnagle et al., 2008; Süssmuth and Mainz, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript describes the substrate selectivity of A domains and cites supporting literature.

claim: Whenever an E domain exists downstream of an A domain, the chirality of the amino acid incorporated into the peptide chain gets modified from L to D.
source: Moreover, whenever an E domain exists downstream of an A domain, the chirality of the amino acid incorporated into the peptide chain gets modified from L to D.
evidence: The manuscript describes the function of E domains.

claim: For most query A domains, rule (1) could be applied (17,880 cases), whereas rules (2) and (3) had to be used rarely (133 and 279 cases, respectively).
source: For most query A domains, rule (1) could be applied (17,880 cases), whereas rules (2) and (3) had to be used rarely (133 and 279 cases, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript reports the frequency of different prediction rules applied.

claim: Six out of the 20 pyoverdine structures had already been elucidated in previous work.
source: Six out of the 20 structures had already been elucidated in our previous work (Rehm et al., 2022), while we here used the same method to elucidate the chemical structure of the remaining 14 pyoverdines (see Supplementary file 13 for MS/MS profiles).
evidence: The manuscript describes which structures were previously known versus newly elucidated.

claim: The UHPLC-HR-MS/MS method was used to elucidate the chemical structures of pyoverdines.
source: We then used the UHPLC-HR-MS/MS method developed in 2022 (Rehm et al., 2022) to elucidate the chemical structures of these pyoverdines.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental method used for structure elucidation.

claim: Valine has been found in a pyoverdine structure but no sequence data from the corresponding strain was available.
source: While citrulline has never been reported in pyoverdines before, valine has been found in a pyoverdine structure but no sequence data from the corresponding strain was available.
